newsitem.title: USA: Scor an unlikely takeover target -- CEO.
newsitem.headline: Scor an unlikely takeover target -- CEO.

text.p: French reinsurer Scor SA is an unlikely target for a takeover even though the global reinsurance industry is going through a period of consolidation, Scor chief executive Jacques Blondeau said.

"We are much more in a position of buying than being sold," Blondeau said in an interview with Reuters on Wednesday. "Especially so, because if you look around, who could be a buyer for Scor?" he asked.
Following a wave of reinsurance mega-mergers last summer, Scor's name has been mentioned occasionally as a possible takeover target.
But Scor, which does about half of its business in Europe, would not be an attractive target for other big European reinsurers like Munich Re and Swiss Reinsurance Co Blondeau said.
And there are not many other reinsurers large enough to acquire Scor, he said, noting that Scor is the sixth largest reinsurer in the world.

"I think the risk (of a takeover), at this stage, is close to nil," he said, noting the strong performance of the company's stock also would likely discourage financial buyers from making an offer for Scor.
Scor American Depository Receipts were trading at 43-3/4 Thursday afternoon in New York, down 1/4 but close to the year's high of 44-1/2.

Despite being the sixth-largest reinsurance company worldwide, Scor's European focus makes it a smaller player in the U.S. market. After its purchase last year of Allstate Corp's U.S. reinsurance business, Scor ranks about 10th in terms of U.S. market share.
However, Blondeau said he expected to see further consolidation in the reinsurance industry, especially in the United States, which he expected to follow Europe's trend.

He noted the number of reinsurers worldwide has already dropped to about 200 from about 480 in 1990, and predicted the number of active reinsurers in the United States would drop by about 50 percent in the next five years.
Last summer, the industry experienced its biggest upheaval with the mergers of several of the world's largest reinsurers.

General Re Corp last year acquired National Re for $940 million, Munich Re acquired American Re for $3.3 billion, and Swiss Re acquired Mercantile & General Re for about 1.75 billion stg ($2.72 billion).
The consolidation followed large catastrophic losses, which pushed customers to seek protection from the larger, more financially-secure reinsurers, he said.
Blondeau said he believes many of smaller reinsurers will simply cease to write new business as they succumb to the market's competitive pressures.
He said the industry may see more deals like Hartford Financial Services Group Inc's agreement last year to acquire the renewal rights to San Francisco Re's property-casualty reinsurance business.
In addition, some insurers with reinsurance subsidiaries have decided to sell those businesses in recent years as part of a strategic restructuring.
Scor, for example, bought Allstate's U.S. reinsurance business last summer as Allstate exited certain non-core businesses.

"I suspect that some of the smaller players are going to disappear. I don't think they are going to be sold because I don't think there are any buyers on the horizon simply because they are too small," he said.
